title: Comparative Anatomy and Evolutionary Relationships Core Test
description: Core practice for compare body structures and development patterns to evaluate evidence for evolutionary relationships.

questions.prompt: What does comparative anatomy compare?
questions.questionText: What does comparative anatomy compare?
questions.correctAnswer: body structures among organisms
questions.explanation: Comparative anatomy uses structure evidence.

questions.prompt: A bat wing and whale flipper share a similar bone order. What claim can this support?
questions.questionText: A bat wing and whale flipper share a similar bone order. What claim can this support?
options: They must do the same job.
They may have related underlying structures.
questions.correctAnswer: They may have related underlying structures.
questions.explanation: Shared pattern can be relationship evidence.

questions.prompt: Why can function alone mislead?
questions.questionText: Why can function alone mislead?
options: Different structures can evolve similar jobs in similar environments.
Function is always unrelated to survival.
questions.correctAnswer: Different structures can evolve similar jobs in similar environments.
questions.explanation: Similar jobs do not always mean close relationship.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports common ancestry?
questions.questionText: Which evidence best supports common ancestry?
options: two organisms are drawn on the same page
several organisms share the same underlying forelimb bone pattern
two organisms have names with the same first letter
questions.correctAnswer: several organisms share the same underlying forelimb bone pattern
questions.explanation: Underlying pattern is stronger than surface association.

questions.prompt: Which model is strongest?
questions.questionText: Which model is strongest?
options: bone pattern -> compare function -> evaluate evidence -> relationship claim
questions.correctAnswer: bone pattern -> compare function -> evaluate evidence -> relationship claim
questions.explanation: The model follows evidence.

questions.prompt: A bird wing and insect wing both fly but have very different internal structures. What should a scientist infer?
questions.questionText: A bird wing and insect wing both fly but have very different internal structures. What should a scientist infer?
options: Similar function alone is not enough to claim close relationship.
questions.correctAnswer: Similar function alone is not enough to claim close relationship.
questions.explanation: Different structures with the same function can be misleading.

questions.prompt: A human arm, cat leg, whale flipper, and bat wing share the same sequence of major bones. What phrase summarizes this evidence?
questions.questionText: A human arm, cat leg, whale flipper, and bat wing share the same sequence of major bones. What phrase summarizes this evidence?
questions.correctAnswer: same pattern, different jobs
questions.explanation: The structures can be modified for different functions.

questions.prompt: A student groups organisms only by whether they swim. What is the weakness?
questions.questionText: A student groups organisms only by whether they swim. What is the weakness?
options: Function is always more reliable than structure.
Swimming is a function or behavior, not enough structure evidence by itself.
Swimming proves no organism has bones.
All swimming organisms are one species.
questions.correctAnswer: Swimming is a function or behavior, not enough structure evidence by itself.
questions.explanation: The grouping needs underlying structure evidence.

questions.prompt: Which data table would help compare anatomy?
questions.questionText: Which data table would help compare anatomy?
options: organisms listed with matching bone positions and functions
organisms listed with no structure data
questions.correctAnswer: organisms listed with matching bone positions and functions
questions.explanation: Structure data supports comparison.

questions.prompt: A fossil limb has the same bone arrangement as several modern forelimbs. Why is that useful?
questions.questionText: A fossil limb has the same bone arrangement as several modern forelimbs. Why is that useful?
options: It proves the fossil is alive.
It removes the need for comparison.
It can connect past and present structure evidence.
questions.correctAnswer: It can connect past and present structure evidence.
questions.explanation: Fossils can extend anatomical evidence through time.

questions.prompt: Which claim overreaches?
questions.questionText: Which claim overreaches?
options: Other evidence can strengthen anatomy evidence.
One similar bone proves the entire family tree with no other evidence.
Similar bone patterns can support a relationship claim.
questions.correctAnswer: One similar bone proves the entire family tree with no other evidence.
questions.explanation: One clue rarely proves a complete tree.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows similar external shape but different internal bone pattern. What should scientists be cautious about?
questions.questionText: A diagram shows similar external shape but different internal bone pattern. What should scientists be cautious about?
options: assuming close relationship from outside shape alone
questions.correctAnswer: assuming close relationship from outside shape alone
questions.explanation: Surface similarity may not match underlying relationship.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would strengthen an anatomy-based relationship claim?
questions.questionText: Which evidence would strengthen an anatomy-based relationship claim?
options: DNA or fossil evidence supports the same grouping
the organisms live in the same zoo
questions.correctAnswer: DNA or fossil evidence supports the same grouping
questions.explanation: Multiple evidence lines are stronger.

questions.prompt: A bat wing is used for flight and a human arm for grasping, but they share a bone pattern. What is the best explanation?
questions.questionText: A bat wing is used for flight and a human arm for grasping, but they share a bone pattern. What is the best explanation?
options: Different jobs mean no relationship is possible.
The wing chose to become an arm.
Related structures can be modified for different functions.
questions.correctAnswer: Related structures can be modified for different functions.
questions.explanation: Structure pattern can persist while function changes.

questions.prompt: Which comparison focuses on underlying structure?
questions.questionText: Which comparison focuses on underlying structure?
options: counting and matching bones in the same positions
questions.correctAnswer: counting and matching bones in the same positions
questions.explanation: Underlying anatomy uses internal arrangement.

questions.prompt: Why are homologous structures useful evidence?
questions.questionText: Why are homologous structures useful evidence?
options: They share an underlying pattern that may reflect common ancestry.
They are made of rock layers.
questions.correctAnswer: They share an underlying pattern that may reflect common ancestry.
questions.explanation: Homologous structures point to relationship through pattern.

questions.prompt: A student says, "Different functions prove the structures are unrelated." Which response is best?
questions.questionText: A student says, "Different functions prove the structures are unrelated." Which response is best?
options: The same underlying structure can be adapted for different functions.
Different function always means no shared history.
Function is the only evidence needed.
questions.correctAnswer: The same underlying structure can be adapted for different functions.
questions.explanation: Different function does not erase shared pattern.

questions.prompt: Which graph pattern would support an anatomical grouping?
questions.questionText: Which graph pattern would support an anatomical grouping?
options: all organisms have the same label length
organisms in the proposed group share more matching structures than organisms outside it
questions.correctAnswer: organisms in the proposed group share more matching structures than organisms outside it
questions.explanation: Shared structure counts can support grouping.

questions.prompt: Why compare similarities and differences?
questions.questionText: Why compare similarities and differences?
options: Both help evaluate how strong a relationship claim is.
questions.correctAnswer: Both help evaluate how strong a relationship claim is.
questions.explanation: Good explanations consider the whole pattern.

questions.prompt: A dolphin fin and shark fin have similar streamlined shapes but different skeletal histories. What idea does this illustrate?
questions.questionText: A dolphin fin and shark fin have similar streamlined shapes but different skeletal histories. What idea does this illustrate?
options: similar function or environment can produce surface similarity without close ancestry
questions.correctAnswer: similar function or environment can produce surface similarity without close ancestry
questions.explanation: Similar environments can favor similar forms.

questions.prompt: Which question pushes beyond memorizing vocabulary?
questions.questionText: Which question pushes beyond memorizing vocabulary?
options: Do these organisms share an internal structure pattern even when the function differs?
How many letters are in anatomy?
questions.correctAnswer: Do these organisms share an internal structure pattern even when the function differs?
questions.explanation: It asks the learner to apply the evidence rule.

questions.prompt: A model tree groups three organisms together because they share a hidden bone pattern. What would be a good next test?
questions.questionText: A model tree groups three organisms together because they share a hidden bone pattern. What would be a good next test?
options: Check whether other evidence supports the same grouping.
questions.correctAnswer: Check whether other evidence supports the same grouping.
questions.explanation: Models improve when tested with more evidence.

questions.prompt: Which is the best evidence-based claim?
questions.questionText: Which is the best evidence-based claim?
options: They are unrelated because their jobs differ.
They are identical because they have limbs.
The shared forelimb pattern supports the idea that these organisms have related structures.
They are related because they both look cool.
questions.correctAnswer: The shared forelimb pattern supports the idea that these organisms have related structures.
questions.explanation: The claim names the evidence and avoids overreach.

questions.prompt: What should a scientist do if structure and DNA evidence disagree?
questions.questionText: What should a scientist do if structure and DNA evidence disagree?
options: Assume DNA always wins without analysis.
Investigate more evidence and revise the model if needed.
questions.correctAnswer: Investigate more evidence and revise the model if needed.
questions.explanation: Conflicting evidence should be investigated.

questions.prompt: A fossil has a partial limb. Why is the claim more limited than with a complete limb?
questions.questionText: A fossil has a partial limb. Why is the claim more limited than with a complete limb?
options: Missing parts reduce how much structure can be compared.
questions.correctAnswer: Missing parts reduce how much structure can be compared.
questions.explanation: Evidence limits affect claim strength.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains adaptation of structures?
questions.questionText: Which statement best explains adaptation of structures?
options: Individuals choose new bones during life.
Inherited structures can change across generations and become suited to different functions.
questions.correctAnswer: Inherited structures can change across generations and become suited to different functions.
questions.explanation: Evolution changes populations over generations.

questions.prompt: A table lists forelimb bone order for five organisms. Four share the same order; one differs. What is a reasonable first inference?
questions.questionText: A table lists forelimb bone order for five organisms. Four share the same order; one differs. What is a reasonable first inference?
options: The four may be more closely related by that structure evidence.
The one that differs is not alive.
questions.correctAnswer: The four may be more closely related by that structure evidence.
questions.explanation: The shared pattern supports a grouping.

questions.prompt: Why should students avoid saying 'same function means same ancestry'?
questions.questionText: Why should students avoid saying 'same function means same ancestry'?
options: Because similar functions can arise from different underlying structures.
Because function never matters at all.
questions.correctAnswer: Because similar functions can arise from different underlying structures.
questions.explanation: Function alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: Which final explanation shows strong understanding?
questions.questionText: Which final explanation shows strong understanding?
options: Shared underlying structures, especially with other evidence, can support evolutionary relationship claims even when functions differ.
One outside similarity proves all ancestry.
questions.correctAnswer: Shared underlying structures, especially with other evidence, can support evolutionary relationship claims even when functions differ.
questions.explanation: This connects structure, evidence, and careful claims.

questions.prompt: Which investigation would best extend the lesson?
questions.questionText: Which investigation would best extend the lesson?
options: Compare limb bone patterns, fossil evidence, and DNA evidence for the same organisms.
questions.correctAnswer: Compare limb bone patterns, fossil evidence, and DNA evidence for the same organisms.
questions.explanation: Using multiple evidence types tests the relationship model.
